A_target.statement:
Let $X$ be a [[Definition:Hausdorff Space|Hausdorff space]].
Then a [[Definition:Sequence|sequence]] in $X$ has at most one [[Definition:Limit Point of Sequence|limit]].

B_source.statement:
Let $\sequence {a_n}$ be a real sequence with $a_n \to L$ and $a_n \to M$.
Then $L = M$: otherwise the intervals of radius $\dfrac {\size {L - M} } 2$ about $L$ and $M$ are disjoint, yet both eventually contain $a_n$.

substitutions.disjoint intervals of radius |L - M|/2: disjoint open neighbourhoods given by the Hausdorff axiom

object_map.reformulation: Keep the disjoint-neighbourhood argument, but obtain the neighbourhoods from the Hausdorff axiom instead of from the metric.

validity_conditions: Without the Hausdorff condition limits need not be unique; in an indiscrete space every point is a limit of every sequence.
The same argument works for nets.
proof_plan: Suppose $x_n \to L$ and $x_n \to M$ with $L \ne M$.
By the Hausdorff property, choose disjoint open $U \ni L$ and $V \ni M$, in place of the disjoint intervals.
Eventually $x_n \in U$, and eventually $x_n \in V$, so some $x_n \in U \cap V = \O$.

This is a contradiction, so $L = M$.
{{qed}}
